passage:
When our tiffin service shut down in my final year, I learned there are many ways people can make you feel worse while trying to help.
My mausi hugged me and said, 'Poor boy, all that effort.' My uncle at a wedding told me I should have done an MBA first, then a business. Someone else mentioned, twice, that my cousin in Pune had just been promoted.
I nodded at all of it. I went home each time feeling smaller.
Hafsa was different. She'd been our first customer. She found me on the library steps a week later and just sat down. 'Tell me what happened,' she said. So I did, all of it, the supplier, the price, the last day. She didn't fix anything. She said, 'That sounds really hard, Nitin.' That was it.
A month later I walked into the placement office for the first time. I think those two hours on the steps are why.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa find Nitin a week after the shutdown?
qa.a: She found him on the library steps.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel after the pity, advice and comparisons from relatives?
qa.a: He felt smaller each time, as if their help pointed out his failure instead of easing it.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's way of helping get right?
qa.a: She listened without judging or fixing, and named how hard it was, which helped Nitin feel steady enough to move forward.

qa.q: How might Nitin's mausi see her own words if she read this account?
qa.a: She might be surprised, since she meant to be kind, and realise that pity made him feel worse rather than supported.

grounding: It shows a young man whose venture failed receiving pity, advice and comparison from relatives, and being helped most by a friend who just listened.

passage:
Counsellor's note, college wellness room. Written by Farida.
Nandini (20) came in on Thursday, two weeks after her CA intermediate results. She said she had failed both groups. She sat with her dupatta twisted round one hand and said she'd come because 'everyone keeps talking at me'.
She listed it quite flatly: her aunt cried and called her 'bechari'; her father forwarded her articles on 'how toppers study'; a neighbour asked, in front of her, whether her cousin had cleared on the first try.
'I know they love me,' she said. 'I just feel like a project now.'
I didn't offer tips. I asked what the last two weeks had been like and let her talk. Near the end she cried, then laughed at herself, and her shoulders dropped.
Next: she has asked to come again next Thursday. I will keep the session for listening unless she asks for planning.

qa.q: How long after her CA intermediate results did Nandini come in?
qa.a: She came in two weeks after her CA intermediate results.

qa.q: What does Nandini mean when she says 'I just feel like a project now'?
qa.a: She feels that her family's pity and advice treat her as something to fix, which leaves her feeling judged rather than loved.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida helped Nandini, and why?
qa.a: Farida gave no tips and let her talk, and that non-judging space let Nandini cry, relax and want to come back.

qa.q: How might Nandini's father see his forwarded articles differently after hearing how she felt?
qa.a: He might understand that his well-meant advice added pressure, and that simply listening could help her more.

grounding: It shows a young woman after a failed exam receiving pity, advice and comparison, and a counsellor whose non-judging listening helps her start to recover.
